---
title: "Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads"
subtitle: "The shared language of routes, the quarterback's feet as a clock, and the one defender every pass play is built to put in a bind."
description: "The numbered route tree and the routes that live off it (seam, wheel, whip, option, sluggo); how the quarterback's drop (3/5/7 steps under center, 1/3/5 from the shotgun) is timed to the depth of the routes; timing routes; progression reads versus defender reads, half-field versus full-field; the high-low (vertical) and horizontal stretches of a single conflict defender; and the numbers that measure a throw: air yards, YAC and aDOT."
glossary:
  "Route tree": "A numbered menu of the basic routes a receiver can run, drawn as branches off one straight stem. In a common version, 1 to 9 run from the flat to the go, odd numbers break toward the sideline, even numbers toward the middle, and the numbers roughly grow with depth. Numbering varies by team."
  "Flat route": "A route to the flat, the area near the sideline within a few yards of the line of scrimmage. The shallowest outside route (the 1 in many route trees)."
  Slant: "A route that takes one to three steps upfield, then cuts sharply inside at roughly 45 degrees into the space between defenders a few yards past the line (the 2 in many route trees)."
  Hitch: {def: "A route that pushes upfield, stops, and turns back to face the quarterback. Short versions (5–6 yards) are usually called hitches; deeper ones (10–14 yards), which turn back toward the middle, are curls, the 4 in many route trees.", aliases: ["Curl route"]}
  Out: "A route that runs straight upfield, then breaks flat toward the sideline: a quick out at about 5 yards, a deeper out at 10–14 yards (the 5 in many route trees)."
  Dig: {def: "A route that runs upfield and then breaks flat across toward the middle of the field, usually 10–15 yards deep (the 6 in many route trees). Shallower versions are often just called in routes.", aliases: ["In route"]}
  "Corner route": "A route that pushes upfield 10–12 yards, then angles toward the sideline and the far corner of the field or end zone (the 7 in many route trees). Also called a flag route."
  Post: "A route that pushes upfield, then angles deep toward the middle of the field, where the goalposts are (the 8 in many route trees)."
  "Go route": {def: "A straight sprint upfield to run past the defender (the 9 in many route trees).", aliases: ["Fly route", "9 route"]}
  Comeback: "A route that sells a deep route for about 15 yards, then stops and comes back toward the sideline and the quarterback (the 3 in many route trees)."
  Wheel: "A route that starts out toward the flat and then turns up the sideline, usually run by a running back or a slot receiver."
  Seam: "A vertical route up the seam, the strip of field between the hash marks and the painted numbers, usually by a slot receiver or tight end, aimed at the gaps between deep defenders."
  Whip: "A short route in which a slot receiver runs at the middle as if on an in-cut, plants, and snaps back toward the sideline. Built to beat a defender who jumps the first move."
  Sluggo: "A double move: a slant fake ('slant and go'), then straight up the field past the defender who bit on the slant."
  "Option route": {def: "A route on which the receiver picks the finish after the snap from what the coverage does: against man he breaks away from the defender's leverage; against zone he settles in the hole between defenders. The quarterback has to see the same thing.", aliases: ["Choice route"]}
  "Drop (3/5/7-step)": "The quarterback's steps backward from the snap to his throwing spot. From under center, 3-, 5- and 7-step drops end roughly 5, 7 and 9 yards deep; from the shotgun, which starts 5 yards back, the same depths take 1, 3 and 5 steps. Each drop is timed to a depth of route."
  "Timing route": "A route the quarterback throws to a spot at a set moment, as his drop ends and often before the receiver has made his break, so the ball and the receiver arrive together."
  Progression: "The order in which the quarterback looks at his receivers on a pass play, usually tied to the steps of his drop: if the first is covered he moves to the second, and so on down to the checkdown."
  "High-low read": {def: "Putting two receivers in one defender's area at two depths, one above him and one below, and throwing to whichever one he leaves.", aliases: ["Vertical stretch"]}
  "Horizontal stretch": "Putting receivers on both sides of an underneath defender (or spread across the field) at about the same depth, so a zone defender can't cover both and the quarterback throws to the one he leaves."
  "Conflict defender": "A defender who is responsible for two things at once (two receivers in his area, or a run gap and a pass zone), so that whatever he does leaves one of them open. Pass plays and RPOs are built around him."
  "Air yards": "How far past the line of scrimmage a pass travels in the air, to the spot where it is caught (or where the target was when it fell incomplete). Throws behind the line have negative air yards."
  YAC: {def: "Yards after catch: the yards a receiver gains after he catches the ball, from the spot of the catch to the end of the play.", aliases: ["Yards after catch"]}
  aDOT: {def: "Average depth of target: the average air yards per pass thrown by a quarterback, or per target for a receiver. How far downfield, on average, the ball is aimed.", aliases: ["Average depth of target"]}
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"
import os
import logging

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrowPatch, Patch
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from IPython.display import Markdown

import gridiron.play as gplay
from gridiron import Play, Player, offense, defense, routes as r, show_animation, style, draw_marker

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
FIELD_W = 160 / 3
ODD, EVEN = style.OFFENSE_DARK, style.THIRD      # outside-breaking vs inside-breaking routes


def no_numbers(ax):
    """Remove the painted yard-line numbers (they sit where receivers stand and crowd the labels)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()


def ruler(fld, play, top=40, fs=6.5):
    """Depth labels (yards past the line of scrimmage) down the left edge of the window, so the
    faint 5-yard lines read as a scale. gridiron has no ruler, so it is drawn here."""
    x_left = FIELD_W - fld.y1 + 0.4
    for d in range(5, top + 1, 5):
        y = play.los + d
        if fld.x0 + 0.8 <= y <= fld.x1 - 0.8:
            fld.ax.text(x_left, y, f"{d}" + (" yd" if d == 5 else ""), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                        ha="left", va="center", zorder=12,
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))


def tag(fld, play, text, at, ha="center", fs=7.0, ec=style.BASELINE, color=style.INK, bold=False):
    """A boxed label at (d, w) yards; `ec` colours the box edge (used to key route families)."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*at))
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, ha=ha, va="center", fontsize=fs, color=color, zorder=12,
                fontweight="bold" if bold else "normal",
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=ec, lw=0.9))


def dotted(fld, play, pts, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.4, arrow=True, head=9):
    """A dotted optional branch through (d, w) points, with an arrowhead."""
    xy = [tuple(float(v) for v in fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*q))) for q in pts]
    xs, ys = zip(*xy)
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=(0, (1, 1.5)), zorder=4)
    if arrow:
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(xy[-2], xy[-1], arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=head, color=color,
                                         lw=0, zorder=4, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))


def faded_route(fld, play, pts, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.6):
    """A route drawn in grey: it is on the play but is not the point of the picture."""
    xy = [tuple(float(v) for v in fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*q))) for q in pts]
    xs, ys = zip(*xy)
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=3, solid_capstyle="round")
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(xy[-2], xy[-1], arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9, color=color,
                                     lw=0, zorder=3, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))


def protect(p, rushers=("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE")):
    """Five linemen set and four rushers engage them: enough to say 'pass', no more."""
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        if k in p.players:
            p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
    for k in rushers:
        if k in p.players:
            p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)


class ball_speed:
    """Temporarily set gridiron's ball speed (yd/s). Its default, 18, is an average over a whole
    flight; a firm 20-30 yard line drive to the sideline travels faster, so the timing figures use
    20-22. Used as `with ball_speed(22): ...` so other figures keep the default."""
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v

    def __enter__(self):
        self.old = gplay.BALL_SPEED
        gplay.BALL_SPEED = self.v

    def __exit__(self, *a):
        gplay.BALL_SPEED = self.old


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- snapshots (print stand-in for video)
def snapshot(play, t, ax=None, lateral=(-6, 26.6), window=(-9, 20), width_in=6.5, notes=(), rings=(),
             show_ruler=False, numbers_off=True):
    """Everyone where he is at time t, faint trails of where they came from, and the ball in flight."""
    pos = {k: play.position(k, t) for k in play.players}
    lo, hi = sorted(lateral)
    moved = [pl.moved(d=float(pos[k][0]), w=float(pos[k][1])) for k, pl in play.players.items()
             if lo + 0.8 <= float(pos[k][1]) <= hi - 0.8]          # drop anyone outside the window
    q = Play([m for m in moved if m.side == "off"], [m for m in moved if m.side == "def"],
             los=play.los, ball_y=play.ball_y, to_go=play.to_go)
    q.highlights = dict(play.highlights)
    for k in rings:
        q.highlight(k)
    fld = q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, width_in=width_in, title=False)
    ax, ppy = fld.ax, fld.pts_per_yard()
    if numbers_off:
        no_numbers(ax)
    if show_ruler:
        ruler(fld, play, fs=5.5)
    P = lambda d, w: fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d, w))  # noqa: E731
    t0 = play._compile()[1]
    for k, pl in play.players.items():
        if pl.pos in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "DE", "DT", "NT"):
            continue
        pts = np.array([play.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(t0, t, 40)])
        if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) < 0.3:
            continue
        xs, ys = P(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
        if pl.side == "off":
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2, alpha=0.5, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=3)
    bx, by = P(*play.ball_position(t))
    thrown = False
    for kind, _, t_rel in play.ball_events:
        if kind == "pass" and t > t_rel:
            thrown = True
            sx, sy = P(*play.ball_position(t_rel))
            ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(sx), float(sy)), (float(bx), float(by)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=8, color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9))
    if not thrown and t > 0 and "QB" in play.players:
        # still in the quarterback's hands: draw it beside him (on the emptier side), not on his "Q"
        qd = play.position("QB", t)
        others = [pos[k] for k, pl in play.players.items() if pl.side == "off" and k != "QB"]
        cands = [qd + np.array([0.0, 1.3]), qd + np.array([0.0, -1.3])]
        best = max(cands, key=lambda c: min(float(np.linalg.norm(c - o)) for o in others) if others else 0)
        bx, by = P(*best)
    draw_marker(ax, float(bx), float(by), "ball", "", ppy)
    for text, at in notes:
        tag(fld, play, text, at, fs=6.3)
    return fld


def strip(plays, times, labels, lateral=(-6, 26.6), window=(-9, 20), notes=None, rings=(), width_in=6.5,
          ncols=3, legend=True, rulers=True):
    """Panels at chosen moments. `plays` is one Play (used for every panel) or one per row."""
    n = len(times)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
    if isinstance(plays, Play):
        plays = [plays] * nrows
    pw = width_in / ncols
    h = nrows * (pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]) + 0.34)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, h), squeeze=False)
    for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t, lab) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times, labels)):
        snapshot(plays[i // ncols], t, ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window,
                 notes=(notes or {}).get(i, ()), rings=rings, show_ruler=rulers and (i % ncols == 0))
        ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=7.8, color=style.INK, loc="left")
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.5, w_pad=0.3)
    if legend:
        h_ = [Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2, alpha=0.6, label="Receiver's path so far"),
              Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="Defender's path so far"),
              Line2D([], [], color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), label="Ball in flight")]
        fig.legend(handles=h_, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=3, fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
    return fig


def show_videos(plays, titles):
    """Web build: several animations side by side in ONE output, so Quarto keeps a single figure
    (two separate show_animation calls would be split into sub-figures)."""
    import shutil
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    from gridiron.animate import animate
    parts = []
    for pl, ttl in zip(plays, titles):
        anim = animate(pl, title=ttl, to_go=pl.to_go)
        if shutil.which("ffmpeg"):
            html = anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
        else:
            html = anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once")
        plt.close(anim._fig)
        parts.append(f'<div style="flex:1 1 300px;min-width:0">{html}</div>')
    display(HTML('<div style="display:flex;gap:8px;flex-wrap:wrap">' + "".join(parts) + "</div>"))
```

```{python}
#| label: data-setup
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (load the passing data used in this chapter)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

SEASONS = range(2021, 2026)          # five completed seasons, 2021-2025
PCOLS = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "play_type", "pass_attempt", "sack", "air_yards",
         "yards_after_catch", "receiving_yards", "complete_pass", "interception", "epa", "success",
         "passer_player_name", "receiver_player_name", "receiver_player_id", "posteam", "down", "ydstogo",
         "yards_gained"]
_raw = pbp(SEASONS, columns=PCOLS)
# Pass attempts that were actually thrown at someone: regular season, sacks out, and only rows
# with a charted air-yards value (spikes and most throwaways have none).
passes = _raw[(_raw.season_type == "REG") & (_raw.play_type == "pass") & (_raw.pass_attempt == 1)
              & (_raw.sack == 0) & _raw.air_yards.notna()].copy()
DEPTH_BINS = [-100, -0.5, 4.5, 9.5, 14.5, 19.5, 29.5, 100]
DEPTH_LABS = ["Behind\nLOS", "0-4", "5-9", "10-14", "15-19", "20-29", "30+"]
passes["depth"] = pd.cut(passes.air_yards, DEPTH_BINS, labels=DEPTH_LABS)

# FTN charting (2022+) says which read each pass went to; participation gives time to throw.
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting([2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]).to_pandas()
ftn["read_thrown"] = ftn.read_thrown.astype(str).str.strip()
part = nfl().load_participation([2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]).to_pandas()[["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "time_to_throw"]]
p22 = pbp([2022, 2023, 2024, 2025], columns=PCOLS)
p22 = p22[(p22.season_type == "REG") & (p22.play_type == "pass") & (p22.pass_attempt == 1) & (p22.sack == 0)]
reads = (p22.merge(ftn[["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "read_thrown", "is_throw_away", "is_screen_pass",
                        "is_qb_out_of_pocket"]],
                   left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"], how="inner")
         .merge(part, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"], how="left",
                suffixes=("", "_p")))

# Numbers quoted in the text
_r25 = reads[reads.season == 2025]
TTT25 = _r25.time_to_throw.median()                                    # median snap-to-throw, 2025
_p25 = passes[passes.season == 2025]
LG_ADOT_25 = _p25.air_yards.mean()
_c25 = _p25[_p25.complete_pass == 1]
YAC_SHARE = _c25.yards_after_catch.sum() / _c25.receiving_yards.sum()
# Throws behind the line: what a completed one gains, and why the group still loses value
_beh = passes[passes.depth == "Behind\nLOS"]
BEH_YDS = _beh.loc[_beh.complete_pass == 1, "yards_gained"].mean()
INT_DEEP = passes.loc[passes.air_yards >= 20, "interception"].mean()
INT_SHORT = passes.loc[passes.air_yards < 20, "interception"].mean()
# EPA of a 4- and a 5-yard gain on first-and-10 (runs and passes, 2021-2025)
_r = pbp(SEASONS, columns=["season_type", "down", "ydstogo", "yards_gained", "play_type", "epa"])
_f = _r[(_r.season_type == "REG") & (_r.down == 1) & (_r.ydstogo == 10) & _r.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"])]
EPA_1ST = {y: _f.loc[_f.yards_gained == y, "epa"].mean() for y in (4, 5, 6)}

_db = pbp([2025], columns=["season_type", "qb_dropback", "shotgun", "play_type"])
_db = _db[(_db.season_type == "REG") & (_db.qb_dropback == 1) & _db.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"])]
GUN_DB_25 = _db.shotgun.mean()                                         # dropbacks from shotgun/pistol
```

Second-and-8 near midfield. The quarterback takes the snap under center, takes five quick steps
backward, plants, hops forward once, and throws toward the sideline, to a patch of grass where
nobody is standing. The receiver he is throwing to is still sprinting straight up the field, with the
cornerback backpedalling in front of him. A beat later the receiver snaps his head around, cuts hard
toward the sideline, and the ball arrives at that patch of grass at the same moment he does, a step
ahead of the cornerback. The analyst says "that's timing." How did the quarterback know where to
throw before the receiver got there? Why five steps and not three or seven? And when the cornerback
*does* get there first, how does he decide to throw somewhere else? This chapter is about the three
things that make every pass play work: the **routes** (where the receivers go), the **drop** (when
the ball comes out), and the **read** (who gets it).

**You'll be able to…**

- Name every route on a replay, by its common name and its number in the route tree, including the
  routes that live off the tree: seam, wheel, whip, option and sluggo.
- Count a quarterback's drop, from under center or from the shotgun, and say roughly how deep the
  throw is meant to be and when it should come out.
- Tell a progression read from a defender read, and a half-field read from a full-field read.
- Find the conflict defender in a high-low (vertical) stretch or a horizontal stretch, and say which
  receiver he left open.
- Read air yards, YAC and aDOT in a box score or a chart, and say what each one tells you about an
  offense.

*Reading the diagrams:* the conventions of
[What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd) (blue circles on offense,
orange squares on defense, a green ring on the player to watch), plus a few that are new here. X is
the wide receiver on the line, Z the one off it, Y usually the tight end, H the third receiver, and
\$ the nickel back (the slot cornerback). Blue arrows are routes. Orange arrows are defenders: **dashed**
when he drops into a zone, **solid** when he runs with a receiver or drives on the ball. A **dotted**
line with an arrowhead is a choice, a path he *could* take; the thin dotted line behind the
quarterback is his footsteps. Grey routes are on the play but not the point of the picture. The
small numbers on the left edge give the depth past the line of scrimmage.

## The passing problem: a race against the rush

A pass play has a clock on it, and the defense controls it: four or more rushers start running at
the quarterback at the snap, and his linemen can't hold them off forever. In the 2025 regular season the median pass left the quarterback's hand
`{python} f"{TTT25:.1f}"` seconds after the snap.[^ttt] Be careful what that number means. It
is not how long the line can hold; plenty of deep throws leave after three seconds, so a good
pocket often lasts longer, and [Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd) measures it. It is how
long quarterbacks *choose* to hold the ball, and they choose short because every extra half-second
is a gamble that the rush hasn't arrived. Two and a half seconds is the working budget: the time
for receivers to get somewhere useful, for the quarterback to decide, and for the ball to leave.

Inside that budget the offense solves three problems at once. **Where:** each receiver needs a
path to open grass, or to a spot where his defender is at a disadvantage; that is his **route**.
**When:** the quarterback must be ready to throw the moment the receiver gets there, not before (the
defender is still close) and not after (the defender has recovered, or the rush has arrived); his
footwork, the **drop**, synchronises the two. **Who:** up to five players can go out, and the
quarterback needs a plan for choosing one in a second or two; that plan is the **read**. Every pass
concept in the rest of Part 4 is a particular answer to those three questions.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In the video game a pass play is five fixed lines, and you choose a receiver by pressing his button
whenever you like. In a real offense a route is a set of instructions that can change with the
coverage and the down and distance, and the quarterback can't wait until a receiver looks open. By the
time a receiver *looks* open on a television screen, it is usually too late to throw it to him. Real
quarterbacks throw to where a receiver is about to be open, on a count their feet keep.
:::

## Anatomy of a route

A route has four parts.

- **The release.** His first steps off the line, getting past the man in front of him. Against a
  [press](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-press) cornerback standing nose to nose with him, who tries
  to *jam* him (hit him with both hands and knock him off his path), the release is a fight of its
  own; [The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd) covers the
  [release](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-release-vs-press) techniques.
- **The stem.** The run upfield before the cut. A good
  [stem](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stem) looks the same for every route, so the defender
  can't tell from it which way the receiver will break.
- **The break.** The cut. Its depth is set by rule ("break at 12 yards", measured from the line of
  scrimmage, not from where he lined up), and its direction names the route. Breaks come in two
  kinds. A *speed* break is rounded, with no plant, to keep the receiver's speed; it suits quick
  routes against defenders guarding areas. A *sink-and-plant* break drops the hips and stops hard,
  to shake a defender running with him; deep outs and comebacks use it, and many coaches have the
  12-yard out break slightly back toward the quarterback rather than dead flat.
- **The finish.** What happens after the cut: keep running away from the defender, stop and face the
  quarterback, or settle in a gap between defenders.

The break is the moment that matters. A receiver can't outrun a defender who is backpedalling in
front of him, but he can make that defender guess. At the break the receiver knows where he is going
and the defender doesn't, so for a fraction of a second the receiver is ahead. That gap, a yard or two
of [separation](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-separation), closes fast. Everything about timing is
about getting the ball there before it does.

## The route tree: a shared language

Receivers and quarterbacks need to talk about routes quickly, in a huddle or with a hand signal at
the line. Most offenses therefore teach a **[route tree](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-route-tree)**:
a numbered menu of the basic routes, drawn as branches off one straight stem. Here is one common
version, for a receiver on the right side of the formation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-route-tree
#| fig-cap: "One common numbered route tree, drawn for a wide receiver on the right of the formation (the ball is at the bottom left, the right sideline at the right edge). Every route starts with the same push straight up the field and splits at a break point. Odd numbers (dark blue tags) break toward the sideline, even numbers (green tags) toward the middle, and the numbers roughly grow with depth. The 0, the hitch, is an addition some systems make. The table beside the tree lists each route's typical break depth, in yards past the line of scrimmage, and its direction."
W0 = 13.0                                    # the receiver: on the line, just inside the numbers
TREE = [  # number, name, absolute (d, w) waypoints after the start, label spot, label alignment
    (0, "hitch", [(6.3, W0), (4.7, W0 - 1.4)], (5.6, 15.6), "left"),
    (1, "flat", [(1.4, W0 + 1.5), (2.4, W0 + 6.5)], (2.4, 20.4), "left"),
    (2, "slant", [(1.8, W0), (6.6, W0 - 6.2)], (6.6, 6.1), "right"),
    (3, "comeback", [(16.0, W0), (13.6, W0 + 3.0)], (13.6, 16.8), "left"),
    (4, "curl", [(12.0, W0), (9.9, W0 - 2.3)], (9.9, 10.0), "right"),
    (5, "out", [(10.0, W0), (10.0, W0 + 6.5)], (10.0, 20.4), "left"),
    (6, "dig (in)", [(14.0, W0), (14.0, 2.5)], (15.6, 2.4), "left"),
    (7, "corner", [(12.0, W0), (22.0, W0 + 7.0)], (23.8, 19.8), "center"),
    (8, "post", [(12.0, W0), (25.5, W0 - 7.5)], (27.0, 5.5), "center"),
    (9, "go", [(29.5, W0)], (31.0, W0), "center"),
]
off = [Player("C", "C", "off", -0.7, 0.0, label="C"), Player("QB", "QB", "off", -5.0, 0.0, label="Q")]
off += [Player(f"R{n}", "WR", "off", -0.7, W0, label="") for n, *_ in TREE]
off[-1] = off[-1].moved(label="X")          # one labelled marker on top of the stack (X: on the line)
tree = Play(off, [], los=35, to_go=None)
for n, name, pts, *_ in TREE:
    tree.route(f"R{n}", pts, absolute=True)
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 4.35))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 2, width_ratios=[1.45, 1.0], wspace=0.04)
ax, axl = fig.add_subplot(gs[0]), fig.add_subplot(gs[1])
fld = tree.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-6, 26.6), window=(-6.5, 32.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, tree, top=30)
for n, name, pts, at, ha in TREE:
    tag(fld, tree, f"{n}  {name}", at, ha=ha, ec=ODD if n % 2 else EVEN, bold=True, fs=7.2)
tag(fld, tree, "toward the middle", (-4.6, 7.0), fs=6.6)
tag(fld, tree, "toward the sideline", (-4.6, 19.0), fs=6.6)
# the cheat sheet beside the tree
CHEAT = [(0, "hitch", "5-6", "stop, face QB"), (1, "flat", "0-3", "out"), (2, "slant", "3-6", "in, 45°"),
         (3, "comeback", "15, back to 12", "back, out"), (4, "curl", "10-14", "stop, face QB"), (5, "out", "10-14", "out, ~square"),
         (6, "dig", "10-15", "in, square"), (7, "corner", "10-12", "out, climbs"), (8, "post", "10-14", "in, climbs"),
         (9, "go", "—", "straight")]
axl.axis("off")
axl.set_xlim(0, 1)
axl.set_ylim(0, 1)
axl.text(0.025, 0.96, "#", fontsize=7.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center", family="DejaVu Sans Mono")
axl.text(0.11, 0.96, f"{'Route':<9} {'Break (yd)':<15} Direction", fontsize=7.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK,
         va="center", family="DejaVu Sans Mono")
for i, (n, name, dep, dirn) in enumerate(CHEAT):
    y = 0.885 - i * 0.07
    axl.text(0.02, y, f"{n}", fontsize=7.6, fontweight="bold", va="center", color=style.INK,
             bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=ODD if n % 2 else EVEN, lw=1.1))
    axl.text(0.11, y, f"{name:<9} {dep:<15} {dirn}", fontsize=7.2, va="center", color=style.INK,
             family="DejaVu Sans Mono")
axl.text(0.02, 0.0, "Box colour: dark blue = odd, breaks toward the\nsideline; green = even, breaks toward the middle.\nDepths in yards past the line; typical, not laws.",
         fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, va="bottom")
plt.show()
```

Two patterns make the tree easy to remember. **Odd numbers break toward the sideline and even numbers
break toward the middle**, and **the numbers roughly grow with depth**. A receiver on the left simply
mirrors the tree, so "breaks outside" always means "toward his own sideline." Each branch exists for a
reason.

- **1, the [flat route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flat-route).** A quick release to the
  *flat*, the strip near the sideline within a few yards of the line. Its job is often to pull a
  defender down and out with it, opening the space above him.
- **2, the [slant](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slant).** One to three steps upfield, then a sharp
  cut inside at about 45 degrees, between the defenders near the line and the ones behind them, with
  the receiver's body shielding the ball from a defender outside him. It is one of the quickest
  routes in football, which makes it a favourite
  [hot route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route): when the defense sends more rushers than
  the line can block, the quarterback throws at once to a receiver running into the space a rusher
  just left ([Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd)).
- **3, the [comeback](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-comeback).** A hard push for about 15 yards to
  sell a deep route, then a stop and a turn back toward the sideline. The more convincing the push,
  the further a cornerback afraid of the deep ball retreats, and the more room there is underneath.
- **0 and 4, the [hitch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hitch).** Push upfield, stop, and turn
  back to face the quarterback. At 5–6 yards it is a hitch (some trees number it 0, many not at all);
  at 10–14 yards, turning back slightly toward the middle, it is a
  **[curl](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-route)**, the 4. Both attack a defender who is
  backing up: against a cornerback 7 or 8 yards off, a 5-yard hitch is open almost by definition.
- **5, the [out](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-out).** Straight up the field, then a cut toward the
  sideline: a *quick out* at about 5 yards, the deeper out at 10–14. It attacks the area outside the
  defenders who guard the middle, and the sideline stops the clock.
- **6, the [dig](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dig).** Up the field 10–15 yards, then a flat cut
  toward the middle, behind the linebackers; shallower versions are often called an
  **[in route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-in-route)**.
- **7, the [corner route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-corner-route).** Up 10–12 yards, then an
  angle toward the sideline and the pylon at the corner of the end zone (hence its other name, the
  *flag*), above a cornerback who stays low and outside a safety who stays in the middle.
- **8, the [post](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-post).** Up the field, then an angle deep toward
  the goalposts in the middle, between deep defenders or behind a safety who has come forward. One
  that angles only slightly inside is a *skinny post*.
- **9, the [go route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-go-route).** A straight sprint, also called a
  **[fly](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fly-route)** or a
  **[9 route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-9-route)**, to outrun the man covering him. Even
  unthrown it does a job: a cornerback running with it is no longer near the short routes. A go that
  drifts toward the sideline is a [fade](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fade), and a ball thrown
  short to his sideline shoulder, so he turns back for it while the defender keeps running, is a
  [back-shoulder throw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-back-shoulder-throw)
  ([Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd)).

**Where the ball sits changes the menu.** The ball is spotted on or between the
[hash marks](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hash-marks), so one side of the formation is usually
wider (the [field side](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-field-side)) and the other shorter (the
[boundary side](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-boundary-side)). Outs and comebacks usually go to the
boundary, where the throw is shorter. A deep out from the far hash to the wide side travels some 30
yards in the air before the cornerback can come down on it, the classic test of a quarterback's arm.
Receivers also keep a sideline rule, finishing their routes about 5–6 yards inside the sideline so an
out, a comeback or a fade has room to land, which is one reason they move their alignment from play to
play, out to [the numbers](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-the-numbers-alignment-landmark) or in to a
[reduced split](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-reduced-split)
([Formation Rules and the Language of Alignment](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)).

**Read the tree in pairs.** A receiver runs one route per play, but his defender has to defend all
of them, and many routes are built to look like another for as long as possible. The slant and the
sluggo (a slant fake, then up the field) start the same way; so do the hitch and the hitch-and-go,
and the post and the post-corner. A cornerback who jumps the first route all afternoon gets the
second. Pairs work across a game, as calls; inside one route, as a double move; and across two
receivers, as the stretches later in this chapter. The idea is the same: make a defender choose, then
throw where he didn't go.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
The tree makes calls short and practice efficient. If every route has a number and a fixed depth, one
digit tells a receiver where to go, and a quarterback and receiver who have run the 5 a thousand times
know, without talking, where the ball will be and when. The cost is rigidity: a number says nothing
about how two routes work together, and a fixed depth is easy to study. So modern playbooks name
*combinations* of routes (concepts), and teach many routes with rules that change them against
different coverages
([Offensive Systems and Play-Calling Languages](04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd)).
:::

### Who numbered the routes, and what a call sounds like

The numbered tree is usually traced to Don Coryell, whose "Air Coryell" San Diego Chargers
(1978–1986) built on Sid Gillman's principle of making a defense cover every yard of the field, and
led the NFL in passing yards six straight seasons from 1978 to 1983 and again in 1985. Numbers let a
play-caller give three receivers their routes in three digits. In the classic version the digits go
to the split end, the tight end and the flanker, in that order, so "896" sends X on an 8, Y on a 9
and Z on a 6: with this chapter's tree, a post, a go up the seam and a dig.[^coryell] It never became
a standard; some trees reverse the odd-even rule or swap the 3 and the 5. "A 9 route" almost always
means a go; most other numbers depend on who is talking.
[Offensive Systems and Play-Calling Languages](04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd) builds the
[digit system](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-digit-system-route-numbering) into full calls.

The names travel better, with dialects: a go is also a fly, a streak or a 9; a dig a square-in; a
hitch a stop; a corner a flag; a skinny post a glance or a bang-8; an option route a choice; a
high-low a hi-lo or "levels". Some systems split the hitch family into a *hook*, which turns straight
back, and a *curl*, which rounds inside.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The receiver runs the route as drawn." Routes are drawn as lines but taught as rules, and the depths
in the tree are targets, not laws. A 12-yard out on third-and-14 is run at 14 yards, past the line to
gain. A receiver who sees a defender sitting on his spot may be taught to adjust, and on some routes
the adjustment is the whole point (the option routes below). The quarterback has to know the rule as
well as the receiver does.
:::

## Off the tree: seam, wheel, whip and sluggo

The tree describes what one wide receiver can do from the outside, with the sideline on one side of
him and the whole field on the other. A receiver inside, in the
[slot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slot) or at tight end, lives in a different place: he has room
to break either way, he is usually covered by a slower linebacker or a nickel back rather than a
cornerback, and he is closest to the deep middle. So inside receivers, and backs who start in the
backfield, have routes of their own, and so do receivers trying to fool a defender rather than simply
get past him. Four come up constantly.

```{python}
#| label: fig-off-tree
#| fig-cap: "Four routes that live off the tree, from a 2x2 formation (the other routes are left off). Left: the sluggo (X fakes a slant for two steps, then runs straight up the field) and the whip (H runs at the middle as if on a short in-cut, plants, and snaps back out). Right: the seam (Y runs straight up between the hash and the numbers) and the wheel (the back runs to the flat, then turns up the sideline, outside the numbers). The wheel needs room, so Z clears it out by running inside (grey)."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [p.moved(w=-17.0) if p.key == "X" else p.moved(w=-8.0) if p.key == "H"
       else p.moved(w=8.0, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=15.0) if p.key == "Z"
       else p.moved(w=2.6) if p.key == "RB" else p for p in off]
ot = Play(off, [], los=35, to_go=None)
ot.route("X", r.path((2.0, 0.0), (4.3, -2.2), (25.0, -2.0)))                 # sluggo: slant fake, then go
ot.route("H", r.path((3.0, -0.6), (4.6, -3.0), (4.2, 3.4)))                  # whip: in, plant, back out
ot.route("Y", r.seam(24))                                                      # seam
ot.route("RB", r.path((0.3, 5.0), (1.8, 11.0), (3.5, 15.0), (6.0, 17.0), (24.0, 17.4)), side=+1)  # wheel
ot.dropback(2.0)
fld = ot.draw(lateral=(-22, 26.6), window=(-7.5, 28.5), title=False)
faded_route(fld, ot, [(-0.7, 15.0), (12.0, 15.0), (24.0, 10.8)])          # Z clears inside for the wheel
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, ot, top=25)
tag(fld, ot, "sluggo (slant-and-go)", (26.8, -15.0), bold=True)
tag(fld, ot, "whip", (1.6, -12.6), bold=True)
tag(fld, ot, "seam", (24.4, 7.6), bold=True)
tag(fld, ot, "wheel", (21.0, 22.6), bold=True)
tag(fld, ot, "Z clears", (26.3, 10.8), fs=6.2, color=style.INK_2)
tag(fld, ot, "hash", (-6.4, -3.1), fs=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
tag(fld, ot, "hash", (-6.4, 3.1), fs=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()
```

- **The [seam](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-seam).** A go route from the inside, straight up
  the strip between the hash marks and the painted numbers. In most deep coverages that strip is the
  seam between the safety in the middle and the deep defender outside, so the route forces the
  defense to decide who takes it: the slot's and tight end's best way to threaten the deep middle.
- **The [wheel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wheel).** Out toward the flat, then up the
  sideline, usually by a back or a slot receiver. A defender who sees a back heading for the flat
  comes forward, and the back turns up the field past him; few linebackers covering a back man-to-man
  can run with him. It needs the sideline cleared, so the outside receiver on that side runs inside.
- **The [whip](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-whip).** A slot receiver runs at the middle as if on
  a shallow in-cut, plants, and snaps back toward the sideline: the harder a man-to-man defender
  drives on the in-cut, the more open the receiver is when he reverses.
- **The [sluggo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sluggo).** "Slant and go": a two-step slant fake,
  then straight up the field, aimed at a defender who has been jumping slants all game. It is the
  best-known [double move](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-move) (a route that shows one
  break and runs another). Double moves take time, so they need protection and usually a pump fake
  (the quarterback starts a throwing motion and holds the ball);
  [The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd) covers the family.

## Option routes: the receiver gets a vote

The tree assumes the receiver knows his route before the snap. On an
**[option route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-option-route)** (also called a
**[choice route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-choice-route)**) he doesn't: he picks the
finish after the snap, from what the defense does. The rule is usually something like this:
"Push to six yards. If one man is following you, break away from him, out if he's inside, in if
he's outside. If the defenders are guarding areas, find the hole between them and sit down, facing
the quarterback."

```{python}
#| label: fig-option-route
#| fig-cap: "One option route, two defenses. The slot receiver (Y) pushes to about 6 yards, then decides. Left, man coverage: the nickel defender (\\$) lines up on Y's inside shoulder to take away the middle and runs with him (solid orange), so Y breaks out, away from him, and the defender is left trailing on his inside hip (the dotted line is the in-cut Y would run if the defender were outside). Right, zone: the defenders drop to areas (dashed) and watch the quarterback, so Y settles in the hole between the Mike (M), who guards the short middle, and the nickel (\\$), who guards the short area outside, and turns back to face the quarterback."
def option_play(man):
    off = [p for p in offense("gun_2x2") if p.key in ("C", "RG", "RT", "QB", "Y", "Z")]
    off = [p.moved(w=8.5, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=16.0) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]
    dfn = [Player("NB", "NB", "def", 1.6 if man else 3.8, 7.6 if man else 11.2, label="$"),
           Player("MIKE", "MIKE", "def", 4.5, 1.5, label="M"),
           Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 7.0, 16.5, label="CB")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    if man:
        p.route("Y", r.path((7.5, 0.0), (8.0, 5.0)))                       # breaks out at 6 yards
        p.path("NB", [(5.6, 8.0), (6.4, 11.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.0, delay=0.25)  # trails, inside hip
        p.path("RCB", [(13.5, 17.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.5)      # carries Z deep
        p.route("Z", r.go(14.5))
    else:
        p.route("Y", r.path((7.5, 0.0), (7.9, -0.8), (7.0, -1.4)))              # sits and turns back
        p.drop("NB", (7.0, 14.2))
        p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
        p.drop("RCB", (13.5, 15.5))
        p.route("Z", r.go(14.5))
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
for ax, man, ttl in ((axes[0], True, "Against man: break away from him"),
                     (axes[1], False, "Against zone: sit in the hole")):
    p = option_play(man)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-3, 21), window=(-7, 16.5), title=False)
    no_numbers(ax)
    y0 = p.players["Y"]
    if man:
        dotted(fld, p, [(5.4, y0.w), (6.8, y0.w - 4.6)], color=style.MUTED)
        tag(fld, p, "$ sits inside:\nY breaks out", (11.6, 4.6), fs=6.4)
    else:
        tag(fld, p, "Y sits in the hole\nbetween M and $,\nturns to face Q", (11.6, 6.0), fs=6.4)
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Why give the receiver a choice? Because the right route depends on the coverage, which isn't settled
until after the snap. Against [man coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-coverage), a
defender on the receiver's inside shoulder is taking away the middle, so the open break is outside,
and vice versa. That position is the defender's
[leverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-leverage-inside-outside), and the receiver, with the
[two-way go](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-way-go) of
[Spread Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd), breaks
away from it. Against [zone coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-coverage), the underneath
defenders watch the quarterback and nobody follows the receiver, so running away from someone is
pointless; he stops in the space between two of them. One call, right against both. Two refinements
are common. Against a man defender lined up
straight in front of him, the receiver stems right at him to make him commit to one side, then breaks
to the other. And many systems tie the choice to the safeties: with one deep safety in the middle
([MOFC](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mofc), "middle of the field closed") he breaks away from his
defender, and with the middle empty ([MOFO](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mofo), "open") he sits;
[Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) explains why.

The cost is that two people must make the same decision in a split second. If the receiver sees
man and breaks out while the quarterback sees zone and throws to where he should have sat down, the
ball goes to nobody, or to a defender, so option routes go to the receivers a quarterback trusts most. The Patriots of the Tom Brady era were famous for building their passing
game around option routes for slot receivers such as Wes Welker and Julian Edelman.[^patriots] Many
other routes carry smaller rules of the same kind ("against two deep safeties, bend the seam into the
middle"), which [Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) collects as
[route conversions](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-route-conversion).

## The drop: the quarterback's feet are a clock

Now the "when." On a *dropback* (any called pass play on which the quarterback sets up behind
his line to throw, including play-action and the ones that end in a sack or a scramble), his feet
follow a prescribed pattern called a **[drop](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-drop-3-5-7-step)**,
counted in steps, and each drop is paired with a depth of route.

From [under center](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-under-center), where he takes the snap with
his hands under the center and starts about a yard and a half behind the line, the classic menu is:

- **Three-step drop**: about 5 yards deep, finished a little under a second after the snap. It goes
  with the quick routes that break at 5–6 yards: hitches, slants, quick outs. The ball should leave
  as his third step lands, with no extra step, more or less as the receiver breaks.
- **Five-step drop**: about 7 yards deep, finished in roughly a second and a half. It goes with the
  intermediate routes at 10–14 yards: outs, curls, digs. The quarterback usually adds a short step
  forward at the end of the drop, a *hitch step* (not to be confused with the hitch route), to
  gather himself, and throws.
- **Seven-step drop**: about 9 yards deep, finished in about two seconds. It goes with the deep
  routes at 15–20 yards and beyond: comebacks, posts, corners, deep digs. It is the slowest drop and
  the one that most needs the line to hold, which is a big reason it is rarer now than in the 1970s
  and 80s.

From the [shotgun](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shotgun), the quarterback starts about five
yards deep, so he needs fewer steps to reach the same depths. The pairs become **one, three and
five steps**: a one-step drop (catch the snap, one step back, throw) for the quick game, three
steps for intermediate routes and five for deep ones. Catching the snap is not a step; count from his
first step back. The pairing of depth and time stays the same.[^drops] On the standard broadcast
angle, high behind the quarterback, watch his feet rather than the ball: count the steps back, look
for the plant of the last one, and then for the small hop forward, the hitch step.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drop-timing
#| fig-cap: "Drops and routes are built as pairs. Left: roughly where the quarterback's last step lands for each drop, measured from the line of scrimmage. Shotgun drops are two steps shorter for the same depth because he starts five yards back. Right: the textbook timing of each pair, in seconds after the snap: the quarterback's drop (blue), his hitch step if the drop has one (light blue), the receiver's run to his break (green, diamond = the break), and the moment the ball should leave (brown ball). On the quick game there is no hitch step: the ball leaves as the last step lands. The black tick on each row is the real median time to throw for passes of that depth, 2023-2025, which runs later than the textbook because many throws are not first-read, on-time throws (the chart on progressions shows why). Textbook depths and times are typical values; they vary by team and quarterback."
_tt = reads[(reads.season >= 2023) & reads.air_yards.notna()].dropna(subset=["time_to_throw"])
TTT_MED = {"quick": _tt.loc[_tt.air_yards.between(0, 9), "time_to_throw"].median(),
           "mid": _tt.loc[_tt.air_yards.between(10, 14), "time_to_throw"].median(),
           "deep": _tt.loc[_tt.air_yards >= 15, "time_to_throw"].median()}

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 3.3))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 2, width_ratios=[1.0, 2.6], wspace=0.08)
axd, axt = fig.add_subplot(gs[0]), fig.add_subplot(gs[1])

# --- left: drop depths
axd.axhline(0, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.4, alpha=0.75)
axd.text(1.0, 0.35, "line of scrimmage", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2)
DEPTHS = {0: [("start", 1.5), ("3-step", 5.0), ("5-step", 7.0), ("7-step", 9.0)],
          2: [("start", 5.0), ("1-step", 6.0), ("3-step", 7.5), ("5-step", 9.0)]}
for x, lst in DEPTHS.items():
    axd.plot([x, x], [-lst[0][1], -lst[-1][1]], color=style.BASELINE, lw=3, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=1)
    for name, d in lst:
        start = name == "start"
        axd.scatter([x], [-d], s=55 if start else 34, color=style.OFFENSE if start else style.SURFACE,
                    edgecolor=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.4, zorder=3)
        axd.text(x + 0.22, -d, name if not start else "QB starts", fontsize=6.6, va="center", ha="left",
                 color=style.INK if not start else style.INK_2)
axd.set_xticks([0, 2], ["Under\ncenter", "Shotgun"], fontsize=7.2)
axd.set_yticks([0, -5, -7, -9], ["LOS", "5 yd", "7 yd", "9 yd"], fontsize=7)
axd.set_xlim(-0.5, 3.6)
axd.set_ylim(-10.2, 1.4)
axd.grid(False)
axd.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
axd.tick_params(axis="x", length=0)
axd.set_title("Where the drop ends", fontsize=8.6)

# --- right: timing
ROWS = [  # key, label, drop end, set/hitch end, throw, break time, route text
    ("quick", "Quick: 3-step\n(gun: 1-step)", 0.95, 0.95, 0.95, 1.0, "routes at 5-6 yd: hitch, slant, quick out"),
    ("mid", "Intermediate: 5-step\n(gun: 3-step)", 1.45, 1.85, 1.85, 1.95, "routes at 10-14 yd: out, curl, dig"),
    ("deep", "Deep: 7-step\n(gun: 5-step)", 1.95, 2.45, 2.45, 2.6, "routes at 15-20 yd: comeback, post, corner"),
]
for i, (key, lab, drop, hitch, throw, brk, txt) in enumerate(ROWS):
    y = -i * 1.25
    axt.barh(y + 0.2, drop, height=0.26, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.9)
    if hitch > drop:
        axt.barh(y + 0.2, hitch - drop, left=drop, height=0.26, color=style.OFFENSE_TINT, edgecolor=style.OFFENSE, lw=0.6)
    axt.barh(y - 0.17, brk, height=0.2, color=style.THIRD, alpha=0.75)
    axt.scatter([brk], [y - 0.17], marker="D", s=30, color=style.THIRD, edgecolor="white", zorder=4)
    axt.scatter([throw], [y + 0.2], marker="o", s=60, color=style.BALL, edgecolor="white", zorder=5)
    axt.plot([TTT_MED[key]] * 2, [y - 0.38, y + 0.42], color=style.INK, lw=1.6, zorder=6)
    axt.text(0.03, y - 0.48, txt, fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, va="center")
axt.set_yticks([-i * 1.25 for i in range(3)], [r[1] for r in ROWS], fontsize=7.2)
axt.set_xlim(0, 3.4)
axt.set_ylim(-3.15, 0.65)
axt.set_xlabel("Seconds after the snap", fontsize=7.5)
axt.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
axt.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
axt.yaxis.tick_right()
axt.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
axt.spines["right"].set_visible(True)
axt.set_title("When the ball should come out", fontsize=8.6)
h = [Patch(color=style.OFFENSE, label="QB drop"), Patch(fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec=style.OFFENSE, label="hitch step"),
     Patch(color=style.THIRD, alpha=0.75, label="receiver to break"),
     Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.BALL, label="ball out"),
     Line2D([], [], color=style.INK, lw=1.6, label="real median, 2023-25")]
fig.legend(handles=h, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.02), ncol=5, fontsize=6.8, frameon=False,
           handlelength=1.4, columnspacing=1.0)
plt.show()
```

Why pair them? Because both are clocks, and the offense wants them to ring together. A receiver
starting from a standstill, with a defender in his way, reaches 5 yards in about a second and 12 in
about two; a quarterback backing up covers his drop on about the same schedule. Matched, the
quarterback's foot lands as the receiver cuts, and the ball leaves without a pause. Mismatched, one of
them waits: a seven-step drop for a hitch hands the cornerback two free seconds to close, and a
three-step drop for a post leaves the quarterback holding the ball while the rush arrives.

The black ticks are a reality check: in 2023–2025 the median throw 10–14 yards downfield left about
`{python} f"{TTT_MED['mid']:.1f}"` seconds after the snap, and the median deep throw about
`{python} f"{TTT_MED['deep']:.1f}"`. Real throws run later because the medians include second and
third reads, scrambles and backs released late. The textbook is the *plan*; the progression data below
show what happens when the plan doesn't work.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Drops turn a judgment ("is he open yet?") into a rhythm ("throw on the fifth step"). A quarterback
who waits to *see* a receiver open is late, because a receiver who looks open has usually been open
for half a second already, and the ball needs another second to get there. A quarterback whose feet
tell him when the receiver will be at his spot can throw before the defender has reacted to the
break. The cost is that a rhythm can be disrupted: a pass rusher in his face, a receiver jammed off
his path at the line, or a defender sitting on the spot breaks the timing. Then the footwork carries
him to his next option: the hitch step that ends the drop is also the moment he moves his eyes to the
second receiver (more under Reads, below).
:::

Three complications. **The shotgun dominates:** in 2025 about `{python} f"{GUN_DB_25:.0%}"` of NFL
dropbacks started from the shotgun or the pistol,[^gun] where the quarterback sees the defense better
and reaches his depth sooner. **Play-action changes the footwork:** a handoff fake comes first, so the
routes are timed to a longer clock ([Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)).
**Not every throw comes off a drop:** quarterbacks roll out and escape a collapsing
[pocket](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pocket), and the routes then follow the scramble rules of
[Quarterback Play](04-07-quarterback-play.qmd).

### Timing routes: throw it before he breaks

Put the pieces together and you get a **[timing route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-timing-route)**:
a route the quarterback throws to a spot at a set moment, as his drop ends and often before the
receiver has made his break. This is the play from the opening paragraph.

```{python}
#| label: fig-timing-route
#| fig-cap: "A timing route: the 12-yard out from a five-step drop under center. The cornerback lines up 7 to 8 yards off Z and, at the snap, backs up to guard the deepest third of the field on his side (a deep third). The ball leaves the quarterback's hand on his hitch step, a tenth of a second before Z breaks toward the sideline, and is thrown to a spot, not to the man. The cornerback can only drive on the ball once Z breaks, so he arrives a step after it. Panels are seconds after the snap (simulated play; Z and the cornerback are ringed; the ball is drawn beside the quarterback until he throws it)."
def timing_out():
    off = [p for p in offense("singleback") if p.key not in ("H",)]
    off = [p.moved(w=14.0) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]       # on the numbers: room for the out
    dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off)
    keep = {"SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE", "MIKE", "WILL", "FS", "SS", "RCB", "LCB"}
    dfn = [p for p in dfn if p.key in keep]
    mv = {"RCB": (7.5, 14.5), "SS": (6.5, 8.0), "FS": (13.0, 0.0)}
    dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1], label="CB" if p.key == "RCB" else None) if p.key in mv
           else p.moved(label="CB") if p.key == "LCB" else p for p in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.block("Y", pts=[(-0.4, 0.3)])
    p.block("RB", pts=[(1.5, 2.2)])
    p.dropback(5.5, speed=3.8)                         # five steps from under center, done at ~1.45 s
    p.path("QB", [(0.8, 0.0)], speed=2.0)              # the hitch step: ball out at ~1.85 s
    p.route("Z", r.path((13.5, 0.0), (13.5, 8.0)), speed=6.9)   # breaks at 12 yards, ~1.95 s
    p.route("X", r.go(20))
    p.path("RCB", [(15.5, 15.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.0)            # backs up into the deep third
    p.path("RCB", [(14.2, 19.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.5, delay=0.45)  # drives once Z has broken
    p.drop("SS", (9.0, 11.0))                          # the short-outside defender gets depth
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, 1.0))
    p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 2.0))
    p.highlight("Z", "RCB")
    p.pass_to("Z", t=1.85)
    return p


def catch_time(play, to, t0, t1=5.0):
    """First moment the ball reaches the receiver (the simulation has no explicit catch event)."""
    for t in np.arange(t0, t1, 0.01):
        if np.linalg.norm(play.ball_position(t) - play.position(to, t)) < 0.05:
            return float(t)
    return t1


tp = timing_out()
with ball_speed(22):
    T_CATCH = round(catch_time(tp, "Z", 1.9), 2)
    _a, _b = tp.pass_target_spot()
    THROW_LEN = float(np.linalg.norm(_b - _a))
TIMES = [0.9, 1.85, 2.45, T_CATCH]
if PDF:
    with ball_speed(22):
        strip(tp, TIMES,
              ["+0.9 s: Z still looks like a go route", "+1.85 s: hitch step, ball out",
               "+2.45 s: Z has broken; the corner drives", f"+{T_CATCH:.1f} s: catch; the corner is a step late"],
              lateral=(-3, 26.6), window=(-9.5, 18.5), rings=("Z", "RCB"), ncols=2, rulers=False, width_in=5.6)
        plt.show()
else:
    with ball_speed(22):
        show_animation(tp, times=TIMES)
```

Follow the cornerback. At 0.9 seconds he is backing up, watching Z run straight at him: this could
still be a go route. At 1.85 seconds the quarterback's hitch step lands and he throws, to a spot near
the sideline 12 yards downfield. Z still hasn't cut. Only when Z breaks, a tenth of a second later,
can the cornerback drive toward the sideline, and by then the ball is on its way. Z catches it at about
`{python} f"{T_CATCH:.1f}"` seconds with the cornerback a step behind.

Why doesn't he break when the ball leaves the quarterback's hand? Because he isn't watching the
quarterback. A defender guarding a deep zone has one job above all, not to be beaten deep, so his
eyes are on the receiver who can beat him, and until Z breaks, an out and a go look the same. (The
underneath zone defenders, with no deep job, are the ones who watch the quarterback.) A cornerback who
guesses early and jumps the out gets beaten by the go: the route tree's pair logic again. Against this
coverage the out usually comes with a flat route from the next receiver inside, to hold the
short-outside defender down; here Y stays in to block, so that defender is free to widen, one more
reason the ball must be on time.

The throw is to a *spot*, and it leaves before the receiver gets there, because it has a long way to
go: some `{python} f"{THROW_LEN:.0f}"` yards from the quarterback's hand to the catch, more than a
second in the air even at the firm 22 yards a second this simulation uses. That makes it hard to
defend and hard to execute: a receiver who is jammed and arrives late, or rounds his cut and arrives
a yard short, turns a completion into an incompletion, or an interception. Coaches have related
words: a
[rhythm throw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rhythm-throw) comes out on the last step of the drop,
with no hitch step ([The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd)), and an
[anticipation throw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-anticipation-throw) is any throw released
before the receiver is open ([Quarterback Play](04-07-quarterback-play.qmd)).

### A short history: Walsh and the three-step game

The modern emphasis on timing owes a lot to Bill Walsh. In 1970 he was an assistant on Paul Brown's
Cincinnati Bengals, and his quarterback, Virgil Carter, was mobile and accurate but had no deep arm.
Rather than ask Carter to throw deep, Walsh built a passing game of short, precisely timed throws,
many off three-step drops, spread across the whole width of the field, so that a pass could do the
work of a running play. Carter led the NFL in completion percentage in 1971.[^walsh] Walsh took the
approach, much refined, to San Francisco as head coach in 1979 and won three Super Bowls with it; its
descendants became the [West Coast offense](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-west-coast-offense)
([Offensive Systems and Play-Calling Languages](04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd);
[Case Study: Bill Walsh's 49ers and the West Coast Offense](../12-case-studies/12-01-walsh-49ers-west-coast.qmd)).

## Reads: what the quarterback is looking at

The routes put receivers in places and the drop sets the moment; the quarterback still has to choose.
He does it with a [read](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-read-post-snap), a decision made
after the snap by watching something specific, in the form "if this, then that." Pass plays use two
kinds of read.

- **A progression read** asks *which receiver is open*, looking at receivers one at a time, in order.
- **A defender read** asks *what is this defender doing*, watching one defender and throwing to the
  receiver he can't cover.

Most plays mix them. A typical call starts with a defender read on one side ("watch the defender
guarding the short area outside; throw the receiver he leaves"), and if both of those receivers are
covered, the quarterback moves on to the next receiver in a progression. One check comes before
either. If the defense sends more rushers than the line can block, the first answer is the
[hot route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route) or a receiver's
[sight adjust](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sight-adjust) (cutting his route short because he
sees the blitz too), thrown at once, before any progression starts.

### Progressions

A **[progression](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-progression)** is the order in which the
quarterback looks at his receivers. The play call gives him a first read, usually the route the play
was designed around; if that receiver is covered, he moves his eyes to the second, then the third,
and finally to the [checkdown](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown), the short, safe throw to
a back or tight end (the *outlet*) that keeps the play from losing yards. Coaches tie each read to
the footwork: the first is thrown on the last step of the drop, the second on the hitch step, the
third after a second hitch, so the progression runs on the drop's clock.

```{python}
#| label: fig-progressions
#| fig-cap: "Two ways to order the quarterback's looks; the green numbers are the progression. Left, a half-field read off a short drop: the play is a two-man combination on the right, a corner route over a hitch (the pair called smash), read high to low off the ringed cornerback, so the corner route is 1 and the hitch 2, with the back released to the flat as the outlet, 3. The routes on the left (grey) are only there to occupy defenders. Right, a full-field read off a deeper drop: a shot at the post on the left, then the dig and the curl across the middle, then the back as the checkdown. Z's go on the right has no number: it is there to clear the cornerback out of the way."
def prog_play(full):
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    off = [p.moved(w=-14.0) if p.key == "X" else p.moved(w=-7.5) if p.key == "H" else
           p.moved(w=7.5, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=14.0) if p.key == "Z" else
           p.moved(w=2.5) if p.key == "RB" else p for p in off]
    dfn = [] if full else [Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 5.5, 16.8, label="CB")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    faded = []
    if full:
        p.dropback(4.0)
        p.route("X", r.post(12))
        p.route("H", r.dig(12, 9))
        p.route("Y", r.curl(12))
        p.route("RB", r.path((2.0, 3.0), (6.5, 4.5)), side=+1)       # checkdown
        faded = [[(-0.7, 14.0), (22.0, 14.0)]]                          # Z: clear-out go
        order = [("1", (24.6, -9.6)), ("2", (12.6, -3.0)), ("3", (12.4, 9.8)), ("4", (1.6, 9.4))]
        drop = ("5-step drop", (-10.5, 0.0))
    else:
        p.dropback(2.5)
        p.route("Y", r.corner(10))
        p.route("Z", r.hitch(5))
        p.route("RB", [(-3.0, 5.0), (0.5, 8.0), (2.0, 11.0)], absolute=True)   # outlet to the flat
        p.highlight("RCB")
        faded = [[(-0.7, -14.0), (1.3, -14.0), (5.0, -9.8)],              # X slant, faded
                 [(-1.5, -7.5), (4.5, -7.5), (4.5, -6.7)]]                # H stick, faded
        order = [("1", (21.6, 13.0)), ("2", (7.4, 11.6)), ("3", (3.6, 9.4))]
        drop = ("3-step drop", (-9.6, 0.0))
    return p, faded, order, drop


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.95))
for ax, full, ttl in ((axes[0], False, "Half-field: one side, 1-2-3"), (axes[1], True, "Full-field: left to right, 1-4")):
    p, faded, order, drop = prog_play(full)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-12.0, 27.0), title=False)
    no_numbers(ax)
    # small panels: enlarge the labelled skill players (marker and letter) so they read in print
    from matplotlib.patches import Circle, RegularPolygon
    for t in ax.texts:
        lab = t.get_text()
        if t.get_fontweight() == "bold" and 1 <= len(lab) <= 2 and lab != "C":
            t.set_fontsize(t.get_fontsize() * 1.4)
            for pa in ax.patches:
                if isinstance(pa, (Circle, RegularPolygon)) and pa.get_zorder() == 8 and \
                        np.allclose(getattr(pa, "center", getattr(pa, "xy", (0, 0))), t.get_position(), atol=0.05):
                    if isinstance(pa, Circle):
                        pa.set_radius(pa.get_radius() * 1.35)
                    else:
                        pa.radius = pa.radius * 1.35
    for pts in faded:
        faded_route(fld, p, pts)
    for n, at in order:
        x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(*at))
        ax.text(float(x), float(y), n, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color="white",
                zorder=13, bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.2", fc=style.THIRD, ec="white", lw=0.8))
    tag(fld, p, drop[0], drop[1], fs=6.6)
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()
```

Progressions come in two sizes.

- **Half-field reads.** The quarterback reads only one side of the field, usually two or three routes
  built to work together there. The other side's routes keep defenders busy, or are an emergency
  answer if the defense blitzes. Because he looks at one side only, the read is quick, which is why it
  fits a short drop. He picks the side before the snap from what he sees: a receiver alone against a
  cornerback playing well off him, or the side with fewer defenders than receivers. Most of the
  quick passing game works this way.
- **Full-field reads.** The quarterback starts on one side, often with a deep route, and works across
  the whole field to the checkdown. A full-field progression gives him more chances to find the one
  mistake the defense made, but moving his eyes and feet across the field takes a deeper drop and
  time the rush may not allow.

The trade is speed versus flexibility. A play-caller picks between them partly on the situation and
partly on the quarterback: a rookie gets more half-field reads; a veteran with a good line gets the
whole field.

#### What the data says about progressions

Since 2022, the charting company FTN has recorded, for every NFL pass, which read in the progression
the ball went to. The nflverse project republishes that charting, so we can see how often
quarterbacks really get past their first look, and what each look is worth in
[EPA](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa), the course's measure of how much a play changed the
offense's expected points ([Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)):
positive EPA left the offense better off than before the snap.

```{python}
#| label: fig-reads
#| fig-cap: "Where the ball actually goes in a progression: FTN's charting of 2022-2025 regular-season pass attempts (sacks excluded) by the read the quarterback threw to. Bar length is the share of attempts; the labels give EPA per attempt and the median time from snap to throw. More than half of all throws go to the first read, and they are both the quickest and the most valuable. Every later look costs time and value; checkdowns are completed most often but are worth about nothing. Designed throws (mostly screens) and scramble-drill throws (made after the play broke down and the quarterback ran around) sit outside the progression. Read codes are interpreted as described in the text."
READ_NAMES = {"1": "First read", "2": "A later read", "CHK": "Checkdown", "DES": "Designed throw (screens)",
              "SD": "Scramble drill", "0": "No read (mostly throwaways)"}
rd = (reads[reads.read_thrown.isin(READ_NAMES)]
      .groupby("read_thrown").agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"), ttt=("time_to_throw", "median"),
                                  comp=("complete_pass", "mean")))
rd["share"] = rd.n / rd.n.sum()
rd = rd.loc[["1", "2", "CHK", "DES", "SD", "0"]]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
ys = np.arange(len(rd))[::-1]
cols = [style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[0], style.MUTED, style.MUTED, style.MUTED]
ax.barh(ys, rd.share, color=cols, height=0.62)
for y, (k, row) in zip(ys, rd.iterrows()):
    ax.text(row.share + 0.008, y, f"{row.share:.0%}   EPA {row.epa:+.2f}   median {row.ttt:.1f} s   "
            f"completed {row.comp:.0%}", va="center", fontsize=6.9, color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks(ys, [READ_NAMES[k] for k in rd.index], fontsize=7.4)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlim(0, 1.0)
ax.set_xticks([0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6])
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_xlabel("Share of pass attempts", fontsize=7.4)
ax.set_title("The progression in the data: early reads are quicker and worth more", fontsize=9)
plt.show()
```

More than half of all throws go to the first read, and they come out fastest and are worth the most:
the first read is the receiver the play was built to get open, thrown on time. Each later look costs
about half a second and a good chunk of the value, and the checkdown, completed most often, is worth
roughly nothing. That is the case for timing in one chart: the offense is at its best when the plan
works the first time.[^ftn]

### Defender reads and the conflict defender

The other kind of read watches one defender instead of a sequence of receivers. The idea is to find
a **[conflict defender](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-conflict-defender)**, a defender who is
responsible for two things at once, and put two receivers in his area. Whatever he does, he is wrong
about one of them. You met this idea in
[What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd), where the quarterback on
Stick reads the slot defender, and the run game uses it on a defender responsible for both a run gap
and a pass zone ([Run-Pass Options](04-06-rpos.qmd)). Defender reads are fast, because the
quarterback looks at one man, not five, and they don't depend on the receivers beating anyone, only
on geometry: a defender can only be in one place. The offense creates the conflict up and down or
side to side.

## The vertical stretch: high and low

A **[high-low read](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-high-low-read)** (also called a
**[vertical stretch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-vertical-stretch)**) puts two receivers in one
defender's area at two depths, one above him and one below. The animation below shows the most common
version, a curl over a flat route, against the defender who guards both in a
[Cover 3](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-3) zone, the
[curl-flat defender](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-flat-defender), who guards the short
area outside, from the flat up to the depth of a curl. (Cover 3 has three deep defenders, each
guarding a [deep third](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-deep-third) of the field's width, and four
underneath; you'll meet it properly in [Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd). For
now all that matters is the one defender.)

```{python}
#| label: fig-high-low
#| fig-cap: "A high-low read of one defender, both branches (simulated play, Cover 3, the right half of the field). Z runs a curl at about 12 yards (high); Y runs to the flat (low). The ringed nickel defender (\\$) is responsible for both areas, so the quarterback watches only him. Top row: he sinks under the curl, so the ball goes to the flat. Bottom row: he jumps the flat, so the ball goes to the curl, behind him and in front of the deep-third cornerback. Times are seconds after the snap."
def high_low(sink):
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    off = [p.moved(w=8.5, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=15.5) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]
    dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off)
    mv = {"RCB": (7.5, 16.0), "NB": (4.5, 10.0), "MIKE": (4.5, 2.0), "FS": (13.0, 0.0), "SS": (5.0, -11.0),
          "LCB": (7.5, -16.0), "WILL": (4.5, -4.0)}
    dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1]) if p.key in mv else p for p in dfn if p.key != "DB"]
    dfn = [p.moved(label="CB") if p.pos == "CB" else p for p in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    p.path("QB", [(0.5, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.route("Z", r.path((12.5, 0.0), (11.2, -1.3)))                     # curl: high
    p.route("Y", r.path((1.0, 3.0), (2.4, 7.5), (3.2, 12.0)), speed=6.4)  # flat: low
    p.path("NB", [(6.5, 11.5)], absolute=True, speed=3.5)               # first steps: shuffle, read
    if sink:
        p.path("NB", [(10.0, 14.0)], absolute=True, speed=4.5)          # sinks under the curl
        p.pass_to("Y", t=1.3)
    else:
        p.path("NB", [(3.8, 17.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.5)           # jumps the flat
        p.pass_to("Z", t=1.7)
    p.path("RCB", [(16.0, 17.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.2)             # deep third
    p.drop("MIKE", (9.0, 4.0))
    p.route("X", r.go(18))                                              # the left side: just occupying
    p.route("H", r.seam(16))                                            # defenders on the web animation
    p.drop("LCB", (15.0, -16.0))
    p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -4.0))
    p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
    p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.5))
    p.highlight("NB")
    return p


HL_SINK, HL_JUMP = high_low(True), high_low(False)
if PDF:
    with ball_speed(22):
        strip([HL_SINK, HL_JUMP], [0.7, 1.3, 2.35, 0.7, 1.7, 2.7],
              ["+0.7 s: $ reads the QB", "+1.3 s: $ sinks; ball to the flat", "+2.35 s: Y catches it",
               "+0.7 s: the same start", "+1.7 s: $ jumps the flat", "+2.7 s: Z catches the curl"],
              lateral=(-2, 26.6), window=(-9.5, 18.5), rings=("NB",), rulers=False,
              notes={1: [("high", (14.3, 11.6)), ("low", (1.8, 23.2))],
                     4: [("high", (14.3, 11.6)), ("low", (1.8, 23.2))]})
        plt.show()
else:
    with ball_speed(22):
        show_videos([HL_SINK, HL_JUMP], ["He sinks: throw the flat", "He jumps the flat: throw the curl"])
```

The ringed nickel's zone runs from the sideline in toward the hash and from the line out to about 12
yards: two receivers' worth of field. If he gets depth to stand under the curl, the flat route is alone in front of him, and the ball goes there
for a few easy yards with room to run. If he comes forward to cover the flat route, the curl settles
in the hole behind him, in front of the cornerback, who is busy guarding the deep third, and the ball
goes there for 10 or 12. The quarterback doesn't need the whole coverage, only one man.

Why does this work? A zone defender is taught to stay between the ball and the deepest threat in his
area, so one who sinks under the curl is doing his job; he is just losing the flat. The defense has
three good answers. It can **change who covers what**: in
[man coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-coverage), each receiver has his own defender, and
there's no one to put in conflict. That is why offenses want a hint of man or zone before they
choose a read, and the defense gives some: the safeties' shell from
[A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd), and
cornerbacks who line up tight, eyes on a receiver, rather than deep and watching the quarterback
([Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) and
[What Beats What](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd) build this out). It can
**pattern-match**: zone defenders pick up a receiver who enters their area and stay with him, so the
curl-flat defender takes the flat and a linebacker gets under the curl
([Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd)). Or it can **bait**: show a soft flat, then
drive on it once the ball is in the air.

The high-low idea is everywhere. In [Cover 2](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-2), two safeties
split the deep field in halves and the cornerbacks stay short, guarding the flats; a corner route
over a hitch puts that cornerback in the same bind (that is the concept called
[smash](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-smash)), and three receivers at three depths on one sideline
make it a three-level stretch (the [flood](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flood) concept). Both
are built in full in [Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd).

## The horizontal stretch: inside and outside

A **[horizontal stretch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-horizontal-stretch)** does the same thing
side to side: it puts receivers on both sides of an underneath defender at about the same depth, so he
can't stand in front of both.

```{python}
#| label: fig-horizontal-stretch
#| fig-cap: "A horizontal stretch. Five receivers settle at 4-6 yards, spread across the field, against the four underneath zone defenders of a Cover 3 defense (dashed arrows are their drops; the two cornerbacks and the free safety drop into the three deep zones). Every underneath defender has a receiver on each side of him. The quarterback watches the ringed Mike, who sits between the back (R) on his left and Y on his right: whichever way he leans (dotted), the man on the other side is open."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [p.moved(w=-16.0) if p.key == "X" else p.moved(w=-8.5) if p.key == "H" else
       p.moved(w=8.5, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=15.5) if p.key == "Z" else
       p.moved(w=-2.4) if p.key == "RB" else p for p in off]
dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off)
mv = {"LCB": (8.0, -16.5), "RCB": (8.0, 16.0), "FS": (13.0, 0.0), "SS": (5.5, -11.0),
      "WILL": (4.5, -4.0), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.5), "NB": (4.5, 10.0)}
```
