```{python}
dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1], label="CB" if p.pos == "CB" else None) if p.key in mv else p
       for p in dfn if p.key != "DB"]
hz = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=8)
protect(hz)
hz.dropback(2.5)
hz.route("X", r.hitch(5))
hz.route("H", r.path((5.5, -0.8), (5.5, -0.2)))
hz.route("RB", [(-1.0, -2.5), (5.5, -2.5)], absolute=True)    # back checks for a blitzer, then sits left of M
hz.route("Y", r.path((5.5, 2.5), (5.5, 3.0)), side=-1)        # Y sits right of M
hz.route("Z", r.hitch(5))
for k, to in (("LCB", (14.0, -16.5)), ("RCB", (14.0, 16.0)), ("FS", (15.5, 0.0)),
              ("SS", (6.5, -12.0)), ("WILL", (7.0, -5.0)), ("MIKE", (7.0, 1.6)), ("NB", (6.5, 11.5))):
    hz.drop(k, to)
hz.highlight("MIKE")
fld = hz.draw(lateral=(-21.5, 21.5), window=(-8, 16.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, hz, top=15)
dotted(fld, hz, [(7.0, 1.6), (7.4, 4.5)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.9, head=13)
dotted(fld, hz, [(7.0, 1.6), (7.4, -1.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.9, head=13)
tag(fld, hz, "M leans to Y:\nthrow to R", (10.6, 6.8), fs=6.6)
tag(fld, hz, "M leans to R:\nthrow to Y", (10.6, -4.0), fs=6.6)
plt.show()
```

The arithmetic is the heart of it. Eleven defenders, minus four rushers, minus the deep defenders,
leaves the underneath ones: 11 − 4 − 3 = 4 in Cover 3, 11 − 4 − 2 = 5 in Cover 2. Put five receivers
across the field at the same depth against four underneath defenders, and at least one receiver has
nobody in front of him while every defender has a receiver on each side. The Mike in the figure stands
in his [hook zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hook-zone), the area just past the line in the
middle, with the back sitting on one side of him and Y on the other. If he leans toward Y, the back
is open; if he leans toward the back, Y is.

Horizontal stretches work underneath, in front of the deep defenders, so they are short, reliable
and quick: the backbone of the quick game's [spacing](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spacing) and
[stick](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stick) concepts ([The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd)).
What they give up is depth; the big gains have to come after the catch. Combine one with a vertical
stretch and you get three receivers around one defender, the
[triangle read](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-triangle-read) of
[Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd).

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Stretches beat zone coverage without winning a one-on-one race. Zone defenders guard areas, and areas
have edges: put two receivers in one defender's area, above and below him or on either side, and he
has to choose. It is Gillman's principle of making the defense cover the whole field, applied one
defender at a time. Against man coverage there is no area to overload, so the answers are different:
routes that win one-on-one, double moves, and crossing routes that make defenders run into each other
(the [man-beaters](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-beater) of
[Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)). That is why "man or zone?" sits behind every read.
:::

## Measuring a throw: air yards, YAC and aDOT

A completion's yards come from two places, the ball's flight and the receiver's run after the catch.
Analytics splits them with three numbers you'll meet on broadcasts and in almost every article about a
quarterback.

- **[Air yards](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-air-yards)** measure how far past the line of
  scrimmage the ball traveled in the air, to the spot where it was caught, or where the target was
  when it fell incomplete. Only the distance downfield counts, not the sideways distance. A screen
  caught 3 yards behind the line has −3 air yards.
- **[YAC](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yac)**, **[yards after catch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yards-after-catch)**,
  is what the receiver adds from the catch to the end of the play.
- **[aDOT](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-adot)**, **[average depth of target](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-average-depth-of-target)**,
  is the average air yards per pass, for a quarterback (per throw) or a receiver (per target),
  completed or not. It describes *where* a quarterback throws or a receiver is used, not how well.

An example. A slant caught 6 yards past the line, and run 14 more: a 20-yard gain, 6 air yards and 14
YAC. An incomplete deep out aimed 14 yards downfield: no gain, but 14 air yards toward the
quarterback's aDOT. Across the NFL in 2025 the average throw traveled about
`{python} f"{LG_ADOT_25:.1f}"` yards past the line, and about `{python} f"{YAC_SHARE:.0%}"` of all
receiving yards came after the catch, so the two halves are close to equal.[^airyards]

```{python}
#| label: fig-depth-value
#| fig-cap: "What each depth of throw is worth, 2021-2025 regular seasons (all pass attempts with a charted target depth; sacks excluded). Short throws are the most common and the easiest to complete, but a completion behind the line of scrimmage loses expected points on average. Completion rate falls steadily with depth while the interception rate (printed inside each completion bar) climbs, yet EPA per attempt rises through about 15-19 yards and then levels off: the deep ball fails often but pays a lot when it hits. The bottom-right panel splits the yards on a completion into the air yards and the yards after the catch."
dv = passes.groupby("depth", observed=True).agg(n=("epa", "size"), comp=("complete_pass", "mean"),
                                                epa=("epa", "mean"), succ=("success", "mean"),
                                                intr=("interception", "mean"))
dv["share"] = dv.n / dv.n.sum()
cmp_ = passes[passes.complete_pass == 1]
dv["air"] = cmp_.groupby("depth", observed=True).air_yards.mean()
dv["yac"] = cmp_.groupby("depth", observed=True).yards_after_catch.mean()
xs = np.arange(len(dv))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.9), sharex=True)
specs = [(axes[0, 0], "share", "Share of all attempts", lambda v: f"{v:.0%}"),
         (axes[0, 1], "comp", "Completion rate", lambda v: f"{v:.0%}"),
         (axes[1, 0], "epa", "EPA per attempt", lambda v: f"{v:+.2f}")]
for ax, col, ttl, fmt in specs:
    vals = dv[col].values
    cols = [style.SERIES[0] if v >= 0 else style.SERIES[1] for v in vals]
    ax.bar(xs, vals, color=cols, width=0.7)
    for x, v in zip(xs, vals):
        ax.text(x, v + (0.012 if col != "epa" else (0.015 if v >= 0 else -0.015)) * (1 if col != "share" else 0.6),
                fmt(v), ha="center", va="bottom" if v >= 0 else "top", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=8.6)
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _, c=col: f"{v:.0%}" if c != "epa" else f"{v:+.1f}"))
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
for x, v, c in zip(xs, dv.intr.values, dv.comp.values):                # interception rate inside the bar
    axes[0, 1].text(x, 0.04, f"INT\n{v:.0%}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=5.6, color="white",
                    fontweight="bold", linespacing=0.95)
axes[1, 0].axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
axes[1, 0].set_ylim(-0.3, 0.55)
axes[0, 1].set_ylim(0, 0.92)
axes[0, 0].set_ylim(0, 0.31)
ax = axes[1, 1]
ax.bar(xs, dv.air, color=style.SERIES[0], width=0.7, label="air yards")
ax.bar(xs, dv.yac, bottom=dv.air.clip(lower=0), color=style.SERIES[2], width=0.7, label="yards after catch")
for x, a, y in zip(xs, dv.air, dv.yac):
    ax.text(x, max(a, 0) + y + 0.8, f"{a + y:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK)
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
ax.set_ylim(-6, 48)
ax.set_title("Yards per completion: in the air + after the catch", fontsize=8.6)
ax.legend(fontsize=6.8, loc="upper left")
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
for a in axes[1]:
    a.set_xticks(xs, list(dv.index), fontsize=6.8)
    a.set_xlabel("Target depth (air yards)", fontsize=7.2)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8, w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

The chart is the passing game's central trade. **Short throws are reliable but don't gain much in the
air, so they live on YAC.** Throws behind the line of scrimmage, mostly screens and flips to backs,
are completed four times in five, and a completed one gains about
`{python} f"{BEH_YDS:.0f}"` yards (about three lost in the air, nine gained after the catch). Yet as a
group they lose expected points, for two reasons. The one in five that falls incomplete wastes a down,
and a six-yard gain is only modest progress: on first-and-10, a four-yard gain averages
`{python} f"{EPA_1ST[4]:+.2f}"` EPA and it takes about five yards to break even
(`{python} f"{EPA_1ST[5]:+.2f}"`).[^first10] That is stricter than the old yardage rule of thumb you met in
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd),
which counts four yards (40% of the ten needed) as a success; the EPA version says second-and-6 is,
on average, a little worse than first-and-10. **Throws of 5–9 yards are the most dependable winners:** completed
about two times in three, they have the highest
[success rate](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-success-rate) of any depth
(`{python} f"{dv.loc['5-9', 'succ']:.0%}"`). **Deep throws fail most of the time and pay anyway.**
Throws of 20 yards or more are completed less than half the time and are intercepted on about
`{python} f"{INT_DEEP:.0%}"` of attempts, against `{python} f"{INT_SHORT:.0%}"` for everything
shorter, yet each attempt is worth about as much as a throw of 10–19 yards, because a completion moves
the ball so far. The bottom-right panel shows a surprisingly steady 3–6 yards after the catch on
anything thrown past the line.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"High aDOT good, low aDOT bad." aDOT describes a style, not a level of play. A quarterback in a quick,
horizontal offense built on YAC can have a low aDOT and an excellent season; a quarterback with a high
aDOT may be taking shots because his team is always behind. YAC has the same problem. It depends on
the play design (screens and crossing routes produce YAC; comebacks and corners rarely do), on the
receiver, and on the throw itself, since a ball placed in stride lets a receiver keep running. To
judge a passer, the course uses measures built on top of these, such as
[CPOE](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cpoe) (completion percentage over expected, which accounts
for depth) in [Quarterback Play](04-07-quarterback-play.qmd), and EPA per play.
:::

The same split shows up in receivers. The table lists the 2025 receivers whose targets were deepest
and the ones who gained the most after each catch.

```{python}
#| label: adot-yac-table
#| output: asis
p25 = passes[passes.season == 2025]
rec = (p25.groupby(["receiver_player_id", "receiver_player_name"])
       .agg(team=("posteam", "last"), targets=("air_yards", "size"), adot=("air_yards", "mean"),
            catches=("complete_pass", "sum"), yac=("yards_after_catch", "sum"))
       .reset_index())
rec = rec[rec.targets >= 80]
rec["yac_per"] = rec.yac / rec.catches
hi_adot = rec.nlargest(5, "adot")
hi_yac = rec.nlargest(5, "yac_per")
nm = lambda row: f"{row.receiver_player_name.replace('.', '. ', 1)} ({row.team})"  # noqa: E731
lines = ["| Highest aDOT | aDOT | YAC/catch | Most YAC per catch | aDOT | YAC/catch |",
         "|:---|---:|---:|:---|---:|---:|"]
for (_, a), (_, b) in zip(hi_adot.iterrows(), hi_yac.iterrows()):
    lines.append(f"| {nm(a)} | {a.adot:.1f} | {a.yac_per:.1f} | {nm(b)} | {b.adot:.1f} | {b.yac_per:.1f} |")
LG_ADOT, LG_YAC = p25.air_yards.mean(), p25.loc[p25.complete_pass == 1, "yards_after_catch"].mean()
lines.append(f"| *League average* | *{LG_ADOT:.1f}* | *{LG_YAC:.1f}* | | | |")
print("\n".join(lines))
print("\n: Two kinds of pass catcher, 2025 regular season: players at any position with at least 80 targets with a charted "
      "depth. aDOT is the average air yards per target; YAC/catch is the average yards gained after the catch. "
      "{#tbl-adot-yac}\n")
```

The two columns are different jobs. The deep-aDOT players are mostly outside receivers on posts, gos
and comebacks, who gain little after the catch because a ball caught 20 yards downfield usually
arrives with a defender close by. The YAC leaders are mostly running backs caught at or behind the
line in open field, where they can make a defender miss. A passing game needs both.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: 49ers 1988 season, Super Bowl XXIII — a progression to the third option"}
January 22, 1989, Miami. The Bengals led the 49ers 16–13 with a little over three minutes left, and
San Francisco took over at its own 8-yard line. Joe Montana drove them 92 yards in 11 plays, mostly
on short and intermediate throws: Walsh's timing game, under pressure. On the final play, from the Bengals' 10 with 39
seconds left, the call, "20 Halfback Curl, X-Up," was designed for the halfback, Roger Craig, with
Jerry Rice in motion to clear out the other side. Craig was held up in traffic, so Montana moved on in
his progression and found John Taylor in the middle of the end zone for the touchdown with 34 seconds
left. San Francisco won
20–16.[^sb23]

**What to notice:** the winning throw went to the receiver the play was *not* designed for. That is
what a progression is for: the first read was taken away, and the quarterback had a pre-set order of
where to look next and the time to look there. It was Walsh's last game as head coach, and the
best-known demonstration of his offense: short, precise, on time, and with an answer when the first
answer was covered.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Buccaneers and Chiefs 2022 — rhythm against improvisation"}
The 2022 season gives the cleanest contrast in modern quarterback timing: Tom Brady's last season in
Tampa Bay and Patrick Mahomes's second MVP season in Kansas City, two prolific passers on very
different clocks.

```{python}
#| label: fig-brady-mahomes
#| fig-cap: "Two ways to beat the clock, 2022 regular season (Brady's last season, Mahomes's second MVP season). Each line is the share of a quarterback's pass attempts thrown in each quarter-second after the snap; the dashed grey line is the league. Brady's throws pile up early, in rhythm. Mahomes throws on time too, but he has a long right-hand tail: about a quarter of his throws left after 3.5 seconds, most of them when the play had moved past its design, and they still produced positive EPA."
q22 = reads[reads.season == 2022]
BM = {}
for _qb in ("T.Brady", "P.Mahomes"):
    _z = q22[q22.passer_player_name == _qb]
    _late = _z[_z.time_to_throw >= 3.5]
    BM[_qb] = {"lt25": (_z.time_to_throw < 2.5).mean(), "first": (_z.read_thrown == "1").mean(),
               "late": len(_late) / len(_z), "late_epa": _late.epa.mean(),
               "late_oop": ((_late.is_qb_out_of_pocket == True) | (_late.read_thrown == "SD")).mean()}  # noqa: E712
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
edges = np.arange(0.5, 6.01, 0.25)
for lab, sel, col, ls in (("League", q22, style.MUTED, (0, (3, 2))),
                          ("T. Brady (TB)", q22[q22.passer_player_name == "T.Brady"], style.SERIES[1], "-"),
                          ("P. Mahomes (KC)", q22[q22.passer_player_name == "P.Mahomes"], style.SERIES[0], "-")):
    tt = sel.time_to_throw.dropna().clip(upper=5.99)
    ax.hist(tt, bins=edges, weights=np.full(len(tt), 1 / len(tt)), histtype="step", lw=2 if ls == "-" else 1.4,
            color=col, ls=ls, label=f"{lab}: median {tt.median():.2f} s")
ax.axvline(3.5, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
ax.text(3.55, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.92, "3.5 s", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlabel("Seconds from snap to throw (throws after 6 s piled into the last bin)", fontsize=7.4)
ax.set_ylabel("Share of attempts", fontsize=7.4)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
ax.set_title("Brady threw in rhythm; Mahomes also won late", fontsize=9)
ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="center right")
plt.show()
```

Brady was the league's model of a rhythm passer: `{python} f"{BM['T.Brady']['lt25']:.0%}"` of his
throws left in under 2.5 seconds, and `{python} f"{BM['T.Brady']['first']:.0%}"` went to his first
read. Mahomes threw on time too, but `{python} f"{BM['P.Mahomes']['late']:.0%}"` of his throws came
after 3.5 seconds, mostly after he had left the pocket or the play had broken down, and those late
throws still averaged `{python} f"{BM['P.Mahomes']['late_epa']:+.2f}"` EPA, better than the league's
average throw.[^bm]

**What to notice:** two answers to the same clock. Brady beat the rush by being done before it
arrived. Mahomes beat it by keeping the play alive after the design ran out, throwing on the run, off
one foot or sidearm to receivers taught where to go when the play broke down (the
[scramble drill](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-scramble-drill) of
[Quarterback Play](04-07-quarterback-play.qmd)). Watch a replay of either and count: on a Brady
throw you can usually match the release to the end of the drop; on many Mahomes throws, the drop is
long over.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: be the route caller"}
Pick one drive and call every pass play three times: before the snap, at the snap, and on the replay.

- **Before the snap: count and number.** How many receivers on each side? Number them from the
  sideline in: #1, #2, #3 ([Spread Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)).
  Note the splits and the hash: a receiver tight to the formation, or on the wide side, has room to
  break outside (corners, outs); one near the sideline mostly breaks inside (slants, digs, posts).
- **At the snap: watch the quarterback's feet.** From under center, count three, five or seven steps;
  from the shotgun, one, three or five, starting after he catches the snap. Three (or one) means the
  ball should be out at once to a 5-yard route; five (or three) means a 10–14-yard route; seven (or
  five), or extra hitch steps, means deep routes or a quarterback working past his first read.
- **Then his head.** If it stays on one side and the ball goes to one of two receivers near the same
  defender, that was a defender read. If it snaps from receiver to receiver, often with his feet
  resetting each time, and the ball goes somewhere he wasn't looking first, he moved through a
  progression.
- **On the replay: name every route.** Use the wide angle that shows the receivers and the deep
  defenders. Name and number each route ("Z ran a 9, H a 5 at twelve, Y a flat, X a slant"), then find
  the stretch: which defender had two receivers in his area, which way did he go, and where did the
  ball go?
- **In the stats:** lots of yards per catch *could* mean deep targets or big YAC; the box score
  can't tell you which. Advanced stat pages (Pro Football Reference, Next Gen Stats) list aDOT and YAC
  separately, and many broadcasts show [Next Gen Stats](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-next-gen-stats)
  graphics (the NFL's player-tracking numbers) with air yards and time to throw.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: count the steps"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-drop
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-10. The quarterback takes the snap under center and drops back: his marker shows where he starts, and the dotted line behind it is his drop, five steps, about seven yards. The cornerback across from Z plays 8 yards off. Z's three possible routes are lettered: A, a hitch at 5 yards; B, an out at 12; C, a post breaking at 14."
off = [p for p in offense("singleback") if p.key not in ("H", "X")]
off = [p.moved(d=-6.5, w=-2.2) if p.key == "RB" else p for p in off]
dfn = [p for p in defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off) if p.key in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE", "SAM", "MIKE", "WILL", "RCB", "FS", "SS")]
dfn = [p.moved(d=8.0, w=15.5, label="CB") if p.key == "RCB" else p for p in dfn]
pr1 = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=10)
pr1.dropback(5.5)
pr1.highlight("Z")
fld = pr1.draw(lateral=(-9, 26.6), window=(-9.5, 27), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr1, top=25)
z = pr1.players["Z"]
dotted(fld, pr1, [(z.d, z.w), (6.0, z.w), (4.6, z.w - 1.4)])
dotted(fld, pr1, [(z.d, z.w), (12.0, z.w), (12.0, z.w + 6.5)])
dotted(fld, pr1, [(z.d, z.w), (14.0, z.w), (24.0, z.w - 6.5)])
tag(fld, pr1, "A", (5.0, z.w - 2.4), bold=True)
tag(fld, pr1, "B", (13.6, z.w + 6.0), bold=True)
tag(fld, pr1, "C", (24.0, z.w - 8.4), bold=True)
tag(fld, pr1, "5-step drop", (-8.0, 3.2), fs=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**You can't see Z's route yet, but you can see the quarterback's feet. Which of Z's three routes is
the ball most likely meant for, and roughly when should it come out?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**B, the out at 12 yards, thrown at about 1.8–2 seconds, around the moment Z breaks.** A five-step
drop from under center ends about 7 yards deep, and it is the drop paired with routes that break at
10–14 yards: outs, curls, digs. The off cornerback is the trap. Eight yards of
[cushion](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cushion) (the space he gives the receiver) *invites* the
hitch, but the hitch (A) goes with a three-step drop; by the time the quarterback finishes five steps,
a 5-yard hitch has been sitting still for a second and the cornerback has had time to close on it. If
the offense wanted the hitch against that cushion, it would have called a three-step drop. The post (C)
needs another second to get open deep; today it is usually a later read off this drop or a shot off
play-action, not the first throw. The cushion still helps the out: a cornerback backing up leaves
room in front of him for a ball thrown to the sideline on time. Footwork is not a guarantee (he can
hitch and work to a deeper second read), but the drop tells you where the *plan* was.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the cornerback who stopped"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-corner
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-8, 1.9 seconds after the snap, against Cover 2 (two deep safeties; the cornerbacks play the short zones near the sideline). On the left, X has run a 5-yard hitch and the slot (H) has pushed to about 10 yards and is breaking toward the sideline on a corner route. The ringed cornerback has stopped about 4 yards deep, just outside X and in front of the hitch, squatting on it; the safety on that side is in the middle of his deep half, 16 yards deep. The ball is drawn beside the quarterback, who still has it."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [p.moved(w=-16.0) if p.key == "X" else p.moved(w=-9.0) if p.key == "H" else p for p in off]
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
mv = {"LCB": (5.0, -17.5), "FS": (12.5, -10.0), "WILL": (4.5, -5.0), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.5), "NB": (4.5, 8.0),
      "RCB": (5.5, 15.0), "SS": (12.5, 10.0)}
dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1], label="CB" if p.pos == "CB" else None) if p.key in mv else p
       for p in dfn if p.key != "DB"]
pp = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=8)
protect(pp)
pp.dropback(2.5)
pp.route("H", r.path((11.5, 0.0), (20.0, 11.0)))                    # high: a real smash corner
pp.block("RB", pts=[(0.8, -1.5)])
pp.route("X", r.hitch(5))                                           # low
pp.path("LCB", [(3.4, -18.6)], absolute=True, speed=3.0)          # squats on the hitch, outside leverage
pp.drop("FS", (16.0, -11.0))
pp.drop("WILL", (8.5, -6.0))
pp.drop("MIKE", (10.0, 0.0))
pp.highlight("LCB")
snapshot(pp, 1.9, lateral=(-26.6, 6), window=(-9, 23), show_ruler=True)
plt.show()
```

**The quarterback is reading the ringed cornerback. Where should the ball go, and why does it have to
go now?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The corner route, to H, thrown now toward the sideline about 18 yards downfield.** This is a
high-low read of the cornerback: X's hitch is the low route, H's corner route the high one. In Cover 2
the cornerback guards the short area near the sideline, and he has done his job, squatting on the
hitch. That leaves the area above him empty until the safety, 16 yards deep in the middle of his half,
can run over and back to it, so the window is open only for a moment: the ball has to leave as H
breaks, over the cornerback's head and in front of the safety. Had the cornerback sunk under the
corner route, the hitch would have been open, and on second-and-8 a 5-yard hitch is a fine result.
This pairing is the
[smash](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-smash) concept, one of the oldest answers to Cover 2
([Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: name the routes"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-routes
#| fig-cap: "Name the routes. Trips right (Z is #1, H #2 and the tight end Y #3), X alone on the left; the back stays in to block. The defense is not drawn: assume Cover 3."
off = offense("gun_trips")
off = [p.moved(d=-1.5, w=6.5) if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(d=-0.7) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]
off = [p.moved(w=17.0) if p.key == "Z" else p.moved(w=11.0) if p.key == "H" else
       p.moved(w=-2.4) if p.key == "RB" else p for p in off]
pr3 = Play(off, [], los=30, to_go=10)
pr3.route("Z", r.go(24))
pr3.route("H", r.out(13.5, 9.0))
pr3.route("Y", r.path((2.0, 3.5), (3.5, 13.0)))
pr3.route("X", r.slant(2, 8))
pr3.block("RB", pts=[(0.5, 1.0)])
pr3.dropback(2.5)
fld = pr3.draw(lateral=(-20, 25), window=(-7.5, 25.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr3, top=25)
for key, at in (("Z", (24.0, 19.5)), ("H", (13.8, 22.2)), ("Y", (3.6, 21.8)), ("X", (7.3, -7.0))):
    tag(fld, pr3, "?", at, bold=True)
plt.show()
```

**Name each route and give its number in the tree from this chapter. Assuming the defense is in
Cover 3, which defender is the play designed to put in conflict, and how should the quarterback read
him?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Z: a go route (9). H: an out (5) at about 12 yards. Y: a flat route (1). X, on the backside: a
slant (2).** The three routes on the right are a three-level vertical stretch along one sideline. Z's
go carries the cornerback deep (if he stays, Z is open deep). That leaves the out and the flat as a
high-low of the curl-flat defender, often the nickel: he is the conflict defender. If he sinks under the out, the flat is open
in front of him; if he comes up for the flat, the out is open behind him. This combination is the
[flood](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flood) concept (also called sail). X's slant is the
[backside](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-playside-backside) answer: if the defense shifts extra
defenders toward the three receivers, or blitzes, X is alone on the other side, and the quick slant
goes to the side the defense left.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **A route has a stem and a break, and the break is where it wins.** The route tree (1 flat, 2 slant,
  3 comeback, 4 curl, 5 out, 6 dig, 7 corner, 8 post, 9 go; odd out, even in) is a shared vocabulary
  whose numbers vary by team; the seam, wheel, whip, sluggo and option route live off it.
- **The drop is a clock.** Three, five and seven steps from under center (one, three and five from the
  shotgun) end at about 5, 7 and 9 yards and pair with routes at 5–6, 10–14 and 15–20 yards. Matched,
  the ball leaves as the receiver breaks; a timing route is thrown to a spot before he gets there.
- **Reads come in two kinds.** A progression checks receivers in order, over half the field (fast)
  or the whole field (flexible, slower); a defender read watches one conflict defender and throws
  where he isn't. First reads are the quickest and most valuable throws.
- **Stretch the defender, up and down or side to side.** A high-low puts receivers above and below
  one defender; a horizontal stretch puts them on either side. Both beat zone by geometry; against man
  the offense needs different answers.
- **Short throws live on YAC, deep throws on air yards.** Air yards, YAC and aDOT describe *where* an
  offense gains its yards, not how good it is. Throws behind the line lose value on average, 5–9-yard
  throws succeed most often, and deep throws fail more but pay.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
- Bill Walsh with Brian Billick and James Peterson, *Finding the Winning Edge* (1997): Walsh's own
  long manual on building and coaching a team, including his offensive philosophy and passing game
  (out of print and hard to find).
- Chris B. Brown, *The Essential Smart Football* (2012) and *The Art of Smart Football* (2015): short,
  clear essays on route combinations, stretches and the history of the passing game.
- Tim Layden, *Blood, Sweat and Chalk* (2010): the stories, told largely by the coaches themselves,
  behind Air Coryell, the West Coast offense and some twenty other schemes.
- Matt Bowen's route-tree primer at the National Football Post (cited below) and his later columns
  for ESPN: a former NFL defensive back explaining routes from the defender's side.
:::

[^ttt]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play joined to `load_participation()`'s
    `time_to_throw` ("duration (in seconds) between the time of the ball being snapped and the time of
    release of a pass attempt"), 2025 regular season, pass attempts with a recorded time (sacks
    excluded). Participation data come from NFL Next Gen Stats through 2022 and from FTN from 2023, so
    times from different eras are not strictly comparable. Dictionary:
    https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_participation.html

[^coryell]: "Air Coryell," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Coryell (Coryell's 12
    seasons at San Diego State before the NFL; his offense "based on Sid Gillman's offense, which
    required the defense to defend the entire field"; the Chargers led the league in passing yards
    from 1978 to 1983 and in 1985). Matt Bowen, "Inside the playbook: the NFL route tree," National
    Football Post (June 30, 2011): https://www.nationalfootballpost.com/inside-the-playbook-the-nfl-route-tree
    (1 flat, 2 slant, 3 comeback, 4 curl, 5 out, 6 dig, 7 corner, 8 post, 9 fade or go, with typical
    depths). Pro Football Hall of Fame biographies of Gillman (Chargers head coach through the AFL
    decade, 1960–1969) and Coryell (San Diego State 1961–1972, Cardinals 1973–1977, Chargers 1978–1986):
    https://www.profootballhof.com/players/sid-gillman/ and https://www.profootballhof.com/players/don-coryell/ .
    The credit for numbering routes rests on the coaching tradition rather than on a documented first
    use; Jason Garrett, a Coryell-system play-caller, describes "the three-digit system of digitizing the
    routes" in Calvin Watkins, "Don Coryell's offense is Jason Garrett's," ESPN Dallas (July 2, 2010):
    https://www.espn.com/blog/dallas/cowboys/post/_/id/4669232/don-coryells-offense-is-jason-garretts .
    The digit order (split end, tight end, flanker) and the example call "896 H-Shallow F-Curl":
    "Play calling system," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_calling_system

[^patriots]: Doug Farrar, "No. 72: Julian Edelman," *Sports Illustrated* (July 12, 2016): "Over the
    last few years, Edelman has replaced Wes Welker as the best option route runner in the NFL":
    https://www.si.com/nfl/2016/07/12/julian-edelman-patriots-nfl-top-100 . For the Patriots' system
    more broadly, Chris B. Brown, "Speak My Language," *Grantland* (Jan. 25, 2013):
    https://grantland.com/features/how-terminology-erhardt-perkins-system-helped-maintain-dominance-tom-brady-patriots/

[^gun]: Course calculation from nflverse 2025 regular-season play-by-play: the share of dropbacks
    with `shotgun == 1` (nflverse marks pistol snaps as shotgun). FTN charting's quarterback-location
    field gives a similar picture (under center on about a third of all 2025 snaps, runs included);
    see `planning/FACTS-current.md` §10.

[^walsh]: "West Coast offense," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_offense (Walsh
    developed the approach as a Bengals assistant under Paul Brown, 1968–1975; Carter, mobile and
    accurate but without a strong arm, "would be the first player to successfully implement Walsh's
    system, leading the NFL in pass completion percentage in 1971"; the three-step drop). "Bill Walsh,"
    Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Walsh (49ers head coach 1979–1988; Super Bowls
    XVI, XIX and XXIII). Pro Football Reference, "1971 NFL Leaders": Carter led with 62.2% (138 of 222):
    https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1971/leaders.htm

[^drops]: Steve Palazzolo, "QBs in Focus: Drop-back Depth," PFF (June 7, 2014): "the 4-6 yard range
    is generally the 3-step game (1 step from shotgun), the 7-8 yard range corresponds to a 5-step drop
    (3 steps from shotgun), and finally the 9+ yard range is more of a 7-step drop":
    https://www.pff.com/news/qbs-in-focus-drop-back-depth . Exact depths vary by coach and quarterback.

[^ftn]: Course calculation from nflverse's republication of FTN charting (`load_ftn_charting()`,
    field `read_thrown`) joined to play-by-play and participation, 2022–2025 regular seasons, pass
    attempts (sacks excluded). The nflverse data dictionary describes the codes as "0" = first read,
    "1" = second read and "2" = third read or later, but that does not match the released files: "0"
    appears on only about 2–3% of 2023–2025 attempts, most of them throwaways, while "1" covers more
    than half of all attempts with the quickest release. This chapter therefore reads "1" as the first
    read, "2" as a later read and "0" as no read, and labels the chart accordingly
    (https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_ftn_charting.html). The release files support
    that reading: "1" has about the same count in 2022 as in 2023–2025 (some 9,300–9,800 attempts a
    season), although the dictionary says first reads are uncoded in 2022; and from 2023 "0" is also the
    value on every run play (in 2022 those are blank), which makes it a fill value, not a read.

[^airyards]: nflverse play-by-play definitions: `air_yards` is the "distance in yards perpendicular
    to the line of scrimmage at where the targeted receiver either caught or didn't catch the ball";
    `yards_after_catch` is the distance "from the yard line where the receiver made the reception to
    where the play ended" (https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_pbp.html). Course
    calculation, 2025 regular season: mean `air_yards` over all pass attempts with a charted depth, and
    the sum of `yards_after_catch` divided by the sum of `receiving_yards` on completions.

[^first10]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2021–2025 regular seasons: mean `epa` of
    all runs and passes on first-and-10 that gained exactly four, five or six yards. Completed throws
    behind the line: mean `yards_gained` on completions with negative `air_yards`, same seasons.

[^sb23]: "Super Bowl XXIII," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXIII (Jan. 22,
    1989, Joe Robbie Stadium, Miami; 3:10 left after the kickoff, a penalty putting the 49ers back at
    their 8; 92 yards in 11 plays; the 10-yard touchdown to Taylor with 34 seconds left; Walsh's last
    game). The call "20 Halfback Curl, X-Up," designed for Roger Craig, with Rice in motion "to clear
    out the back side": *The Philadelphia Inquirer*, "Taylor makes amends with the winning catch"
    (Jan. 25, 2008):
    https://www.inquirer.com/philly/online_extras/20080125_TAYLOR_MAKES_AMENDS_WITH_THE_WINNING_CATCH.html ;
    the snap with 39 seconds left, with Walsh diagramming the play: FootballScoop,
    https://footballscoop.com/watch-legendary-bill-walsh-diagram-explain-play-won-super-bowl-23 .
    Taylor's own account names Craig, Rice and himself as "the three options": San Francisco 49ers,
    "75 for 75: The Drive":
    https://www.49ers.com/news/75-for-75-the-drive-joe-montana-super-bowl-xxiii-cincinnati-bengals

[^bm]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, FTN charting and participation (Next Gen
    Stats time to throw), 2022 regular season, pass attempts by Brady and Mahomes (sacks excluded).
    "Left the pocket or the play broke down" counts throws charted by FTN as out of the pocket or as
    scramble-drill throws. Among the 29 passers with 300 or more 2022 attempts with a charted target depth, Brady had the
